\chapter{Eight Words, Read Rather Than Recognised}
\label{ch:ur-script-seven}
\hlchaptermodality{16}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can read salam, kya, kan, nak, lal, kala, nila and lena letter by letter from the right rather than from the romanization, and explain why Urdu leaves its short vowels unwritten.}

Eight words the book had only ever given by ear, read letter by letter from the right -- including kan and nak, the same three letters in different orders, which is the proof that the reader is decoding rather than recognising. Every letter the reading needs was taught back in chapters one to five.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Practice]{Practice — eight words you already knew, now read}

\label{lesson:UR-C16-practice}



\begin{quote}
Write the seven letters this reading needs — \ur{ا،} \ur{ل،} \ur{س،} \ur{م،} \ur{ک،} \ur{ن،} \ur{ی} — in a row, right to left, naming each as you go, and let the line fall as it travels.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the words come back}
\textbf{Nothing new is taught here.} Every word below was already given to you to say, and every letter in it is one you can now write.

Read each from the right, naming its letters before you say it:

\begin{quote}
\ur{سلام}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{کیا}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{کان}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{ناک}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{لال}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{کالا}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{نیلا}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\ur{لینا}
\end{quote}

\emph{salām} — \emph{kyā} — \emph{kān} — \emph{nāk} — \emph{lāl} — \emph{kālā} — \emph{nīlā} — \emph{lenā}.

Eight words from seven letters. Two of them are worth a second look: \textbf{\ur{کان}} \emph{kān} \textquotedblleft{}ear\textquotedblright{} and \textbf{\ur{ناک}} \emph{nāk} \textquotedblleft{}nose\textquotedblright{} use the \textbf{same three letters} in different orders, which is the clearest possible proof that you are reading rather than recognising a picture.

\begin{culture}
Count the letters in \textbf{\ur{کیا}} and count the sounds in \emph{kyā}.

\textbf{Urdu writes its long vowels and leaves the short ones off the page.} The reader supplies them. That is why \emph{salām} has a vowel between the s and the l that nothing on the page records.

This has a consequence worth accepting now rather than discovering later: \textbf{you cannot reliably sound out an Urdu word you have never heard.} Reading and listening have to grow together here, more tightly than in a language that spells every vowel — which is exactly why this book put every one of these words in your ear, chapters before it asked you to read one.
\end{culture}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter}]
Seven letters you have been carrying since chapter five, and three ideas that outlast them:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{the page runs right to left}, and in Nastaliq the word also \textbf{falls} as it goes, each letter hanging below the last
  \item \textbf{letters join}, changing shape by position — but the change is a \textbf{trimming}, and \textbf{alif refuses to join leftward}, which is what puts gaps inside a word
  \item \textbf{what is added matters}: nūn's dot, kāf's slash, and ye's bare curve are the identification, not the decoration
\end{itemize}

Seven of Urdu's letters. The rest are mostly more of what you just did.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \ur{کان} and \ur{ناک} — same three letters, and say which is which
  \item \emph{Write it:} \ur{سلام} — and let it break after alif
  \item \emph{Read it:} \ur{کالا} \ur{نیلا} \ur{لال} — name the letters of each before saying it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of your seven letters refuses to join to the left? (\textbf{\ur{ا}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
